**Base rate.** The closest Czech precedents favor renewal, but the sample is small. The cabinet continued the spring fuel caps into May and renewed the autumn caps on October 26, six days before the November rules took effect. It also let the spring caps end on July 19 when market conditions improved. That makes another extension plausible, not automatic. **What moves this forecast.** On November 13, Finance Minister Alena Schillerová said a decision was needed within a week to ten days, a timetable that points to November 23. On November 19, Prime Minister Andrej Babiš told reporters the cabinet had not considered the extension because Schillerová was absent, not because it had rejected it. Both facts favor a Monday decision. The Finance Ministry’s November 20 update still cited supply risks, which favors renewal, though its diesel ceiling had fallen to CZK 44.53 per litre from CZK 48.69 on October 26, weakening the case for keeping the caps. The regulation in force is Government Decree No. 203/2026 Sb., which sets maximum petrol and diesel prices and a CZK 2.50/l retailer-margin cap only through 30 November 2026. The cabinet meets on Monday 23 November at 11:00, but the published ODok programme for that sitting does not contain a fuel-price item, and no December decree is in VeKLEP.

Base rate: this year’s two review points split. The spring regime was ended in late June once wholesale prices stabilised; the October regime was extended on Monday 26 October, five days before expiry, when the Finance Ministry said the oil-market shock had not eased. Same-day filing of the decree is a proven path.

Facts that move this case: Schillerová said on 13 November that a December decision was due within a week to ten days, so Monday is the outer edge of her own timetable. The 19 November sitting skipped the item only because she was in Brno. ČTK on 20 November said the cabinet might decide as early as Monday. The ministry’s page, updated 20 November, still cites Hormuz tanker and infrastructure risks even after Yanbu loadings resumed. Against extension, the caps themselves have fallen hard (petrol to 39.47 Kč/l, diesel to 44.53 Kč/l for 21–23 November), the diesel excise waiver costs about CZK 1.1 billion a month, and the refinery levy meant to offset it is still only in second reading.

Strongest reason the obvious “they will extend on Monday” reading fails: the criterion is not whether the caps survive past November, but whether an approving regulation or resolution is taken inside 22–23 November. Deferral to the Monday 30 November sitting, a mid-week meeting after the 26–27 November European Council, or a decision to let the decree lapse are all NO. Prices have already given the cabinet the same “stabilisation” cover it used in June, and nothing on the published agenda locks the item in for Monday.

### 3. Strongest Reason the Obvious Outcome Might Fail
Given that the extension is absent from the Ministry of Finance's pre-published materials for 23 November and fuel prices have dropped below 40 CZK/l for petrol, the most likely outcome is **NO** (either because the government decides on 23 November to let the regulation expire on 30 November, or because it defers the formal vote/adoption of a decree to the Monday 30 November cabinet meeting).

The strongest reason this **NO** outcome might fail (resulting in a **YES**) is that Prime Minister Babiš's statement on 19 November and Minister Schillerová's statement on 13 November show that the political discussion on whether to continue the regulation is slated for the 23 November cabinet meeting. In Czech cabinet practice, time-sensitive crisis measures or straightforward technical rollovers of existing decrees (which only require changing the date range from November to December) can be brought by a minister directly to the table as an urgent addendum (*dodatek k programu* / *mimo pořad*) following coalition consultations on Monday morning. Furthermore, Schillerová has repeatedly praised the price caps and diesel tax cut for keeping Czech inflation at 2.1% (as recently as 20 November 2026), and coalition partner SPD (via Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik) strongly favors continuing the regulation to protect hauliers before Christmas. If the coalition agrees on Monday morning to maintain the anti-inflationary shield for one more month, the cabinet can approve the decree on the spot on 23 November and publish it in the Collection of Laws that afternoon.

Balancing the clear absence of a draft decree from the 20 November MF agenda release and falling fuel prices against Babiš's 19 November indication that the matter awaited Schillerová's return and the government's strong populist/anti-inflationary incentives, I estimate a 28% probability that an extension is approved within the 22–23 November window.
